text: James Lusk Alcorn (November 4, 1816 – December 19, 1894) was a governor and U.S. senator during Mississippi’s Reconstruction era. A Moderate Republican and Whiggish "scalawag," he faced a bitter rivalry with Radical Republican Adelbert Ames, who defeated him in the 1873 gubernatorial race. Alcorn was the first elected Republican governor of Mississippi. Born near Golconda, Illinois Territory, to James Alcorn and Hanna Lusk, a Scots-Irish family, he studied at Cumberland College in Princeton, Kentucky, and practiced law in Salem, Kentucky, where he was admitted to the bar in 1838. He served in the Kentucky House of Representatives in 1843 and moved to Mississippi the following year. He established a law office in Coahoma County, where his property holdings and law practice grew, making him wealthy. In 1850, he built a three-story house at Mound Place Plantation in Coahoma County. By 1860, he enslaved nearly one hundred people and held lands valued at a quarter of a million dollars. He served in the Mississippi House of Representatives and Senate during the 1840s and 1850s as a leading Whig. He founded the levee system and was chosen president of the levee board; a levee district was established in 1858 through his efforts. He ran for Congress in 1856 but lost, and in 1857 was nominated for governor by the Whigs but declined. Alcorn attended the 1851 Mississippi convention called by Democratic governor John A. Quitman, who advocated secession, and joined the Mississippi Unionists to oppose secession, warning of a Northern-dominated South. However, in January 1861, he joined the secessionists and was elected to the Committee of Fifteen to prepare the Ordinance of Secession. Though born in the free, pro-U.S. state of Illinois, he joined the Confederate States of America and was appointed brigadier-general of the Mississippi Militia. Jefferson Davis refused to commission him due to political differences, and Alcorn served in the Confederate Army for about eighteen months in inconspicuous field duties, mainly raising troops and garrison duty. After several major generals resigned, including Davis, Earl Van Dorn, and Charles Clark, Alcorn became eligible for promotion but was passed over because John J. Pettus was governor. At the start of the Civil War, Alcorn was ordered to central Kentucky and later stationed at Fort Donelson, Tennessee. In October 1861, he raised three regiments of militia, designated the Army of 10,000, and led them to Camp Beauregard, Kentucky, under General Leonidas Polk. His field service ended in January 1862 when his brigade was disbanded. He was captured in Arkansas in 1862, paroled later that year, and returned to Mound Place Plantation. In 1863, he was elected to the Mississippi state legislature, where he joined critics of Confederate President Jefferson Davis. During the war, he spent a fortune raising and supplying troops; in 1863, his plantation was raided during the Yazoo Pass Expedition. He preserved part of his wealth by trading cotton with the North. In November 1863, he wrote to his wife that he had sold 111 bales of cotton, holding ten thousand dollars in Green backs and one thousand in gold. After the war, he was among the fifty wealthiest men in the South. He lost two sons to the war: Milton Stewart Alcorn, who committed suicide in 1879 after returning home partially deaf and a drunkard, and Henry "Hal" Alcorn, who ran away to join the military, became ill, was captured, and died of typhoid fever en route to Mississippi. Alcorn was elected to the U.S. Senate in 1865 but was barred from seating due to his participation in the Confederacy. He supported suffrage for freedmen and endorsed the Fourteenth Amendment. He led the scalawags, who made up about a fourth of Republican officials in Mississippi, in coalition with carpetbaggers and freedmen. Most Republican votes came from African Americans, despite most state officeholders being white. In the 1869 election, Alcorn defeated Lewis Dent to become governor, serving until 1871. As a modernizer, he appointed former Whigs, some previously Democrats, supported public schools for all, and established a new black college, now known as Alcorn State University, which he helped shape with Hiram Revels as its president. Many Republicans opposed him due to his patronage and resistance to civil rights legislation, as well as his unwillingness to appoint local Black officers when white alternatives existed. He opposed a state civil rights bill and believed in preserving the old Southern civilization. Alcorn resigned to become a U.S. senator from 1871 to 1877, succeeding Hiram Revels, the first African American senator. As a senator, he advocated for removing political disabilities of white Southerners, rejected federal efforts to end segregation in hotels, restaurants, and railroads, denounced the federal cotton tax as robbery, and defended separate schools for races. Though a former enslaver, he described slavery as "a cancer upon the body of the nation" and expressed satisfaction over its end. His estrangement from Adelbert Ames deepened in 1871, and by 1873, their rivalry turned into intense animosity. Ames won the 1873 gubernatorial race by 69,870 to 50,490 votes, defeating Alcorn, who won support from scalawags. Alcorn withdrew from state politics and accused Ames of being incapable and an enemy of the people. When Blanche Bruce was elected as the second African American senator in 1874, Alcorn refused to introduce him to the Senate, and Bruce was welcomed by Roscoe Conkling. In 1875, during a period of rising violence against Black Republicans, Alcorn led a white force against Black Republicans at Friar's Point, resulting in at least five Black deaths. Alcorn supported modernizing the South while believing in white supremacy and advocating civil and political rights for African Americans. In a letter to his wife, he stated that white Southerners must make African Americans their friends or the future would be "red with blood and damp with tears." He founded the Mississippi levee system and played a key role in rebuilding levees after the Civil War. After retiring from politics, he remained active in levee affairs, served as a delegate to the 1890 Mississippian constitutional convention, where he supported the black disenfranchisement clause introduced by Democrats. He was twice married: first in 1839 to Mary C. Stewart, who died in 1849, and in 1850 to Amelia Walton Glover of Alabama. In later life, he practiced law in Friars Point, Mississippi, and lived quietly at Eagle's Nest in Coahoma County. He died in 1894 and was buried at Eagle's Nest in the Alcorn Cemetery in Friars Point. He commissioned a statue of himself, which was placed on his grave. Alcorn County, Mississippi, and Alcorn State University, the first historically black land-grant university, are named in his honor.
